1:
Who Lemuel was divides them, and one refuses the majority. John Gill reports three answers: a later king, which he answers from the arrangement of the book; a foreign prince, perhaps in Chaldea, since Chaldee words occur three times in his mother’s address; and the general sense of Jewish and Christian writers, that he is Solomon. Matthew Henry takes the last, noting that the name means one devoted to God and answers to the name given by divine appointment, and that the same writer tells elsewhere what his father taught him, though he allows the conjecture of a neighbouring prince whose mother was of Israel. John Wesley assents by general consent. Charles Ellicott reads it Lemuel, king of Massa, and says the identification with Solomon has no good reason. Adam Clarke says plainly that he cannot receive it, on two grounds: the son is called the son of my womb, which suits a first-born and not the child of a woman who had been another man’s wife; and the son of my vows, which intimates a lawful marriage. He also divides the first words differently, taking the particle as a preposition, so that these are words spoken to the king, not by him.

On the mother the comment turns respectful. Henry draws the duty, that mothers as well as fathers must teach their children, who while young are most under the mother’s eye; and adds that even kings must be catechised, the greatest of men being less than the least of the ordinances of God. Ellicott sets the passage in Eastern manners, where the mothers of kings received the title of queen-mother, which he thinks explains why the mothers of the kings are so constantly named; and in his own day, he adds, the mother of the ruler of Egypt ranks before his principal wife.

The broken exclamation that follows is filled out four ways. Gill hears her asking what she shall call him and confessing that she wants words and wisdom, and reports two versions that make her reprove instead. Wesley reads a heart too full to begin. Ellicott counts the repetitions, three questions showing her anxiety for a son only beloved in her sight. Clarke calls the verse very elliptical, notes that commentators have inserted whole sentences to make the sense, and quotes an old English version supplying: my son, thou son of my body, O my dear beloved son. Henry makes it a chiding question, since she had observed his inclination to women and wine.

The two warnings raise a crux and a custom. At the clause about what destroys kings, Keil and Delitzsch observe that the pointing allows an infinitive, so that it might mean, direct not thy ways to the wiping out of neighbouring kings; but they refuse it, since such a warning will not parallel one against spending strength on women. Ellicott reaches the same end by a change of pointing, yielding those who destroy kings, that is, the women; Clarke notes only the foreign termination on the word. At the strong drink for him that is ready to perish, Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott report the same custom: on the ground of these words the women of the city prepared a drugged draught for those condemned to death, which was offered to Jesus and refused, because he would not pass from life insensible to his suffering; Clarke reports it briefly. Gill turns the verse into almsgiving, kings giving the drink away out of their abundance to those in starving circumstances rather than drinking it themselves. On the dumb all agree that no natural infirmity is meant but the man who cannot plead for himself through ignorance or awe of the court; Gill adds that the Hebrew name for a widow comes from dumbness, and Clarke lists the renderings for those appointed to destruction, indigent travellers, the desolate, or orphans.
10:
The acrostic is noticed at once, and raises a question of authorship. Adam Clarke sets it out plainly, that from this verse each one begins with a consecutive letter of the alphabet, and divides the piece in three, the general character, its particulars, and the summing up. Matthew Henry counts the twenty-two verses and observes that the alphabetical form, as in some of the Psalms, makes some think this no part of the mother’s lesson but a poem by itself, commonly repeated among the pious Jews and made alphabetical for ease of remembering; he finds its abridgment in two apostolic passages on the duty of wives, and adds the proverb that he who will thrive must ask his wife leave. John Gill reports that two versions detach the passage and a scholar makes it another hand’s composition, and offers the compromise that the mother gave the substance and the son the form. John Wesley notes the alphabetical order.

Who the woman is divides them further. Gill holds that the description is drawn to such a pitch that it can agree with no daughter of fallen Adam taken literally, neither with the queen mother nor with the Virgin. Charles Ellicott lists the mystical identifications held at different times, the Law, the Church and the Holy Spirit, without adopting any. Clarke keeps to the plain sense and glosses the opening word, a woman of power and strength, full of mental energy, whose worth no precious stones can equal.

The husband who shall have no need of spoil produces a crux. Keil and Delitzsch explain that the word properly means what is taken from an enemy but came to mean gain of any kind, and reject a scholar who makes it the husband’s prosperity, since the word denotes the gain and not the feeling that goes with it; the gain meant is what the housewife brings in. Ellicott renders it that he shall have no lack of gain, his incomings increasing from her prudent care. Clarke takes the older sense literally: her husband is not obliged to go out on predatory excursions to provide for his family at the expense of the neighbouring tribes. Wesley makes it that he need use no indirect courses to get wealth. At the next verse Keil and Delitzsch praise the constancy rather than the deeds, since her love is not dependent on freaks but rests on deep moral grounds; Clarke puts it in a phrase, that for kind words she returns kind deeds.

The wool and flax turn two of them to antiquity. Gill collects the great personages who did such work, the matron whose husband came from the camp and found her spinning with her maids, and a king’s wife so excellent a spinster that her wool and distaff were long kept in one temple and a garment of her making in another; whence, he says, came the custom of leading newly married women home with a distaff carried before them. Clarke draws the economic point, that she did not buy ready woven cloth but procured the raw material, wool from her own flocks and flax from her fields, and adds that women of the highest rank worked with their hands. Keil and Delitzsch dispute the verb, which five scholars render that she handles wool and flax; the Hebrew word, they say, describes not the external working at a thing but the mind’s intention directed to it, so that she cares to bring the material in. On the merchant ships Clarke keeps the trade exact: if she buys she sells enough of her own manufacture to pay for it, and if she imports she exports. Ellicott and Wesley make it thrift, buying cheaply at a distance rather than paying more on the spot; Keil and Delitzsch admire the reach of it, a calculating look that goes beyond the nearest circle to descry distant opportunities of exchange.
15:
The rising before day is read as management. Adam Clarke makes her an economist of time: when the nights are long the household works into the evening and rises before daylight, so that the day’s food is prepared and the labour not interrupted; and he distinguishes the two things given out, food for those going to the fields, a word taken from hunting, and a task for the women within, fixing the kind of work, the material and the quantity expected of each, so that everything is done orderly. Charles Ellicott notes the same double sense, that what is given the maidens may be their allotted provisions or their allotted work. Keil and Delitzsch place her exactly: she is up before the other inmates though not before the maids, because care for her house stands above her own comfort, or rather because that care is to her a satisfaction. John Gill compares the rising while it was dark to Christ rising to pray; John Wesley says only that she distributes all necessary provisions.

At the field the commentary turns to household economy. Clarke supposes a growing family needing more land, a neighbouring field on sale, an estimate of its worth and a good bargain, paid for by her own industry; the vineyard she plants supplies beverage, medicine and sacrifice, and barter rather than buying is her chief mode of traffic. Keil and Delitzsch suggest the field is one hitherto wanting to the family rather than an addition to lands they hold, since the poet has in view a woman whose husband is no landlord but has a business in the city. Gill leaves the ground entirely, making the field the Scriptures, which the enlightened will buy at any rate and never sell. Ellicott and Wesley keep to the saving and the improving. Keil and Delitzsch then follow the produce past the needs of the house: what is over is brought to sale, and the gain stimulates the diligence of the unwearied woman, which is why she girds herself with strength as with a girdle. Clarke reads the girding as care of her health, since she avoids what might enervate the body or soften the mind.

The lamp that does not go out draws the sharpest remark in the chapter. Clarke offers three explanations, that a light burning all night was of great advantage against sudden alarm where there were so many banditti, that some work may have been carried on at night by those who slept in the daytime, so that labour never stood still, and then his own protest, that little children are often so employed now to support indigent parents and to fill the coffers of their unfeeling taskmasters. Wesley will not press the candle at all, taking it to signify only her unwearied care. Keil and Delitzsch make the halves of the verse antecedent and consequent, since she comes to taste how profitable her industry is and is spurred to redoubled effort.

At the spindle the technical detail is divided between two of them. Keil and Delitzsch describe the whorl, the ring fixed on the spindle to give it weight and regulate its movement, and give its names in three languages. Clarke describes the operation instead: the distaff held in the guard of the left arm, the thread drawn down by the fingers of the left hand and twisted by the right; and the spindle and distaff, he observes, are the most ancient of all instruments for making thread, superseded first by the wheel and then by machinery. Gill notes that a queen of the Greek poems did so too. Wesley draws the conclusion nearest home, that though such employments have grown out of fashion among great persons in these delicate times, they were not so in former ages, and that this is why unmarried women are still called in the language of our law spinsters.
20:
The outstretched hand is read as gift by two, as alliance by one. Adam Clarke notices that the first clause has the singular and the second the plural, so that with one hand she relieves the poor in general and with both she gives to the afflicted poor; and adds that God requires a portion for the poor out of every man’s gain, without which his blessing is not on the rest. Charles Ellicott allows sympathy or alms. Keil and Delitzsch deny that alms are in view: what impels her is not a narrow-hearted care for her own circle but a love reaching beyond it, and the hand she holds out is offered as if for an alliance, as if she said, place confidence in me, there thou hast my hand; they reject a scholar who imagines an open palm with a gift in it, since the word means the half-opened hand.

The scarlet clothing divides them three ways. Ellicott keeps the colour and makes it part of the comfort, since scarlet by its very hue suggests warmth. Keil and Delitzsch keep it too, from a root meaning to shine, and observe that snow in the rainy season is not rare there and is sometimes accompanied by intense cold, so that she looks on winter without fear. Clarke refuses the colour: it can do nothing to keep off cold and would be improper wear for the bogs and dirt of winter; the word comes from a root meaning to double and signifies double garments, a rendering the translators themselves put in the margin. John Wesley says only that she has provided not merely for necessity but for delight and ornament.

At the coverings and the purple Clarke turns antiquarian, then sceptical. He takes the coverings for carpeting on which guests may sit and quilted work for the beds, and identifies her clothing with the fine linen of one country, which he has often seen wrapping mummies and likens to our coarse calico; then he comes to the purple, supposed to be dyed with a liquor from a large shellfish of which he has seen specimens nearly two feet long, and doubts whether any such liquor was ever got from that or any other fish, holding the story invented to hide the trade secret. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the bedding, giving four old renderings of the word, one of which makes the coverings shaggy on both sides. John Gill reports a version rendering it garments of divers colours, like the coat of the patriarch’s son.

The husband in the gates is agreed on, and traced to the same cause. Keil and Delitzsch say that such a wife advances the estimation in which her husband is held, so that he has a reputable name where the affairs of the city are deliberated and a weighty voice among the elders; they also note the wavering pointing of the word for known. Clarke says he is respected not only for the neatness of his dress but as the husband of a woman universally esteemed, and that her management gives him leisure for the civil interests of the community. Ellicott puts it as a contrast, that instead of hindering her husband’s advancement she furthers it, since having no domestic anxieties he is free for public life. Gill reports two Jewish commentators, one making him known for the garments she made him, the other for his wisdom. At the last verse Keil and Delitzsch render that she prepares body-linen and sells it and delivers girdles to the merchants of the coast, and spend their note on the word for linen, which may come from a distant country’s name and which the Talmud uses of a light garment worn next the skin. Gill reports a commentator who makes it a covering for the night, and a version that names the city she sells to.
25:
Her clothing of strength and honour is expounded as security. Keil and Delitzsch define both words: strength is power over the changes of circumstance which easily shatter a household resting on less solid foundations, and glory is elevation above what is low and common; so that her raiment is a just pride with which she looks confidently into the future. Charles Ellicott makes the same point of the figure, that she never parts with these, which serve her like clothing for protection and ornament, and renders the second clause that she smiles at the coming day. Adam Clarke reads the verse of her workmanship: what she makes has a double perfection, being strong and elegant, so that she will never have occasion to blush for anything she has made, worn or sold. John Wesley takes the strength for magnanimity and courage, and the laughter for a constant tranquillity of mind resting on the providence of God. John Gill takes it of the church, weak in herself and strong in her Lord.

The opening of her mouth is where the praise turns inward, and one voice says so. Keil and Delitzsch call it one of the most beautiful features in the portrait, and explain that wisdom is the means by which she breaks the silence of her mouth; they distinguish what lies under the tongue, ready to be spoken, from what is on the tongue and in the act of being spoken, and take the phrase as a genitive of property, against a scholar who reads it as instruction directed towards kindliness. Clarke and Ellicott both use the verse to deny that she is a drudge: she has not neglected the cultivation of her mind, says Clarke, and is conciliating in her manners; she is no mere household drudge with no thought beyond food and clothing, says Ellicott, but cares for the higher interests of her family, kindness being the law by which she regulates her words. Wesley marks both extremes she avoids, being neither sullenly silent nor full of impertinent talk, and explains why the practice is called a law, because it is constant and customary and proceeds from an inward principle.

On the household and the rising up the comment turns practical. Clarke makes a religious industry the law of her house, and adds the reason for the feeding: she knows that idleness leads to vice, so that everyone has his work and everyone his proper food, and that they may work well they are fed well. Gill reads the same oversight ecclesiastically, that all things be done decently and in order, the feeble supported and the incorrigible cast out. Keil and Delitzsch spend their note on the word for ways, which elsewhere means the things needed for a journey, and in one plural form magnificence, but originally the walk, and here the comings and goings of a house. Wesley says only that she observes the whole carriage of children and servants.

At the last of these verses Keil and Delitzsch announce the finale of the poem, and read the rising up as carrying the idea of reverential honour: the children bless her for having brought the house to such prosperity and to a state in which love reigns, and the husband rises in his turn and sings her praise. Clarke puts the cause first, that she considers a good education next to divine influence, so that her children are well bred and taught the fear of the Lord; and he notices what the husband is doing, showing himself sensible of her excellence and encouraging her by the commendations he bestows. Gill reports a Jewish note that the children rise in the morning, her lamp not having gone out in the night, and another that takes the children for disciples.
29:
The husband’s closing tribute raises one question of translation and one of application. Keil and Delitzsch refuse the rendering that makes the many daughters gainers of riches, which six authorities adopt, since it would give the encomium at its height a mercenary note, and since the phrase bears that sense only when it is joined to a preposition of the person; what is meant is bravery and moral energy. John Gill reports the same versions without rejecting them, and then turns the daughters into false churches, many where the true church is one. Charles Ellicott glosses the word simply as women, a term of affection. Adam Clarke assigns the verse to the husband and renders the second line that she has ascended above the whole of them, carrying every duty and every excellency to a higher perfection than any of whom we have read or heard; and then he steps out of the commentary altogether to say that he has met at least her equal, the daughter of one divine and the wife of another, the rector of a country parish.

The summing up divides on who is speaking. Keil and Delitzsch hold that what follows is not a continuation of the husband’s praise, as three scholars take it, but the poet’s own closing sentence, confirming the husband’s words by referring them to their general ground: grace is deceit because a man who estimates a wife merely by the loveliness of her appearance is deceived by it, and beauty is vanity because it is nothing that remains but falls under the law of all material things. Clarke works the same two words harder. Grace of manner, he says, may be a mere semblance and outward varnish, learned by painful drilling in polished seminaries and lasting only while the restraint lasts, an outside at which the inside murmurs; and beauty of shape and countenance is impaired by sickness, deranged by suffering and destroyed by death. John Wesley makes comeliness often a cover to a deformed soul, which does not give the satisfaction it promised and is soon lost by many diseases and contingencies as well as by death. Ellicott says only that outward graces do not last, and that enduring praise belongs to those who fear the Lord. Gill applies the deceitful favour to the meretricious dressings of the church he opposes, and reports a Jewish commentator who refers the words instead to the grandeur of the kings of the nations.

The last verse is read as a command, as a prayer and as a promise. Keil and Delitzsch explain the fruit of her hands as the good her conduct has brought to maturity, the blessing she has secured for others and, by the promise, for her own enjoyment, and they reject a proposed emendation of the opening word. Clarke suggests that the line may be a prayer rather than a charge, that she may long enjoy the fruit of her labours; and he ends by wishing her example held forth in the most public places and set before every wife and mother, that they may learn from it what men have a right to expect, closing his comment with an Amen. Gill reports two Jewish readings, one making the words the husband’s charge to the children and the other referring the whole to the world to come, when the graces of believers will be found to praise and honour. Wesley leaves the verse to itself.
